audience: Beginning linear algebra students working in the plane R^2. They already see a 2x2 matrix as a motion of the grid, know that its columns are the images of e1 and e2, and can compute A v. This film builds on that picture to explain what the product of two matrices means.
assumed: A linear map of R^2 is fully determined by where it sends e1 and e2
The columns of a matrix are the images of e1 and e2 (column 1 = A e1, column 2 = A e2)
Computing a matrix-vector product A v and reading it as moving the vector v
Seeing a 2x2 matrix as a motion of the whole grid: grid lines stay straight, parallel and evenly spaced, and the origin stays fixed
Recognising R = [[0,-1],[1,0]] as a 90° counterclockwise rotation and S = [[1,1],[0,1]] as a horizontal shear
central_question: If we do one linear map and then another, what single matrix describes the combined motion, and does the order matter?
opening: An empty dark frame with only the fixed text panel on the right third: a dark backing rectangle with a thin border, still empty.

scenes.title: Rotate, then shear
scenes.purpose: Doing one linear map after another is again a motion of the whole plane that keeps grid lines straight, parallel and evenly spaced and leaves the origin fixed. So it is a single linear map, and it should have a single matrix.
scenes.shows: A coordinate grid fades in on the left with e1 (green) and e2 (red) drawn from the origin and labelled. The panel shows R in blue. The whole plane turns smoothly through a quarter turn, driven by one angle tracker. Hold. S appears in gold in the panel, to the left of R, and the already rotated plane shears horizontally by blending the matrix entries from the identity. Hold. Then the plane smoothly undoes both motions back to the starting grid, and a faint muted ghost copy of the original grid stays underneath. The grid then moves in one continuous motion straight from the original to the final sheared-and-rotated position by blending the identity into the combined matrix. It lands exactly where the two-step motion landed. Its lines are still straight, parallel and evenly spaced over the ghost, and the origin has not moved. A teal matrix bracket with two empty columns appears in the panel next to S R, standing for the single matrix still to be found. The ghost fades out.
key_points: First the rotation acts, then the shear acts on the rotated plane
The end result is still a grid with straight, parallel, evenly spaced lines and a fixed origin
So the two motions together form one linear map, and one direct motion reaches the same final grid
That raises the question: which matrix is it?
elements: grid: the plane, now in its final rotate-then-shear position
e1: green basis arrow at its final position, labelled
e2: red basis arrow at its final position, labelled
R: blue rotation matrix in the panel
S: gold shear matrix in the panel, written to the left of R
SR_bracket: empty teal matrix bracket in the panel, waiting for its columns
scenes.ends_with: The grid sits in its final rotate-then-shear position, with green e1 and red e2 at their final positions. The panel shows S and R side by side, next to an empty teal matrix bracket.

scenes.title: Follow e1 and e2
scenes.purpose: Because the composite is linear, its matrix comes from watching where e1 and e2 finally land. Reading off those two arrows gives SR without any product formula.
scenes.shows: The grid fades to a fainter shade so that only the two basis arrows stand out. Then the plane smoothly undoes the motion back to the identity. Now the two-step motion replays, one arrow in focus at a time, and each arrow leaves a thin muted trail. Under the rotation, e1 swings up to point straight up. Under the shear it slides sideways to the diagonal. e2 swings to point left under the rotation. When the shear plays, e2 stays perfectly still, because it lies on the horizontal axis. A soft pulse on e2 marks that stillness. The coordinates of the two final arrow tips appear briefly beside them. Then they move smoothly into the empty teal bracket in the panel as its first and second columns, in green and red, so the bracket becomes SR. The trails and the tip coordinates fade, and the grid returns to its normal brightness.
key_points: Only two arrows need to be tracked, not every point
e1 ends at the diagonal: it is rotated up, then sheared sideways
e2 ends pointing left: it is rotated, then left alone by the shear because it lies on the x-axis
Where e1 and e2 land are the columns of the composite matrix SR
elements: grid: the plane in the rotate-then-shear position
e1: green arrow at its final position
e2: red arrow at its final position
R: blue matrix in the panel
S: gold matrix in the panel
SR: teal matrix in the panel, with a green first column and a red second column
scenes.ends_with: The grid is in the rotate-then-shear position with e1 and e2 at their final positions. The panel shows S and R, and next to them the filled teal matrix SR with a green first column and a red second column.

scenes.title: One hop equals two hops
scenes.purpose: The product of two matrices is defined as the matrix of the composite map, so that (BA)v = B(Av) for every v. The single matrix SR does in one step what R and then S do in two.
scenes.shows: The plane smoothly undoes the motion back to the identity. A yellow sample vector v appears and is labelled. Route one: the plane rotates, and v rides along to Rv. Pause. Then the plane shears, and v ends at S(Rv). A small muted marker stays at that tip. The plane smoothly undoes the motion again. Route two: the plane moves in one direct motion by blending from the identity to SR, and v travels straight to its new place. It lands exactly on the marker, which then fades. In the panel the equation (SR)v = S(Rv) appears under the matrices. While route one is recalled by a brief highlight, the right-hand side glows. While the single hop is recalled, the left-hand side glows. After that only the equation stays. The general statement (BA)v = B(Av) is then written below it, and v fades out.
key_points: Two hops, R and then S, take v to S(Rv)
One hop with the single matrix SR takes v to the same point
The product is defined by exactly this agreement, for every v: (BA)v = B(Av)
elements: grid: the plane in the rotate-then-shear position
e1: green arrow at its final position
e2: red arrow at its final position
R: blue matrix in the panel
S: gold matrix in the panel
SR: teal composite matrix in the panel
definition: (SR)v = S(Rv) with (BA)v = B(Av) below it, in the panel
scenes.ends_with: The grid is in the rotate-then-shear position with e1 and e2 at their final positions. The panel shows S, R and the teal SR, and below them the definition (SR)v = S(Rv) and (BA)v = B(Av). The vector v is gone.

scenes.title: Columns of A carried by B
scenes.purpose: Column i of BA is B applied to column i of A. This is what the plane already showed. It also rules out entry-by-entry multiplication.
scenes.shows: In the panel, R's first column glows green: it is where the rotation sent e1. A copy of that column moves next to S, giving S times the column, and the multiplication resolves to the diagonal vector. That vector moves into the first column of SR, which glows to confirm it. On the grid, e1 pulses at the same moment, to show that it is the same arrow. Then the same thing happens in red for the second column: S leaves it unchanged, it goes into column 2 of SR, and e2 pulses. The helper copies disappear. Next, a muted wrong matrix made by multiplying R and S entry by entry appears in the panel. A muted outline of the grid it would produce fades in over the plane. It clearly does not match the grid we watched, so a cross is drawn over the wrong matrix, and the matrix and its outline fade away. Finally the general rule appears in the panel under the definition: column i of BA = B (column i of A).
key_points: Column 1 of R is where e1 went first. S carries it on to column 1 of SR
Column 2 of R is where e2 went first. S carries it on to column 2 of SR
Multiplying entry by entry gives a grid that does not match the composite motion
The rule: column i of BA = B times column i of A
elements: grid: the plane in the rotate-then-shear position
e1: green arrow at its final position
e2: red arrow at its final position
R: blue matrix in the panel
S: gold matrix in the panel
SR: teal composite matrix in the panel
rules: the definition (BA)v = B(Av) and the column rule, in the panel
scenes.ends_with: The grid is in the rotate-then-shear position with e1 and e2 at their final positions. The panel shows S R = SR with the teal matrix, and below it the definition and the column rule. No helper copies or wrong matrices remain.

scenes.title: The matrix next to v acts first
scenes.purpose: In BA, the matrix written next to the vector acts first. So BA means first A, then B: read it from right to left.
scenes.shows: To simplify the panel, the rules from the last scene fade out and the expression S R v appears, with v in yellow on the far right. The plane smoothly undoes the motion back to the identity. A small arrow under the expression starts at v and moves right to left. When it reaches R, R glows blue and the plane rotates. Pause. When it reaches S, S glows gold and the plane shears. The arrow fades, and S R v turns into SR v with the teal matrix. On the grid, the order in which the motions played matches the right-to-left order of the symbols. The general statement BA = first A, then B is shown only through symbols: under B A, small arrows point right to left, with an A in the first position and a B in the second.
key_points: v sits on the right, so the matrix next to it, R, touches it first
S acts second, on the result
SR means 'rotate, then shear', read from right to left
elements: grid: the plane in the rotate-then-shear position
e1: green arrow at its final position
e2: red arrow at its final position
S: gold matrix in the panel
R: blue matrix in the panel
SR: teal composite matrix in the panel, labelled SR
scenes.ends_with: The grid is in the rotate-then-shear position with e1 and e2 at their final positions. The panel shows S R = SR in teal, with a small right-to-left arrow under S R.

scenes.title: Shear, then rotate
scenes.purpose: Doing the motions in the opposite order gives a different final grid and a different matrix, RS, which is not SR. Order matters.
scenes.shows: The current plane shrinks smoothly into the left half of the geometry area. It keeps its rotate-then-shear position and its teal label SR. A second plane fades in on the right half at the identity, with its own green e1 and red e2. On the right, the shear plays first: e1 stays still on the axis and e2 tilts to the diagonal. Pause. Then the rotation plays: e1 swings up to point straight up, and e2 swings to the upper left. The left plane stays still the whole time, so there is only one motion at a time. In the panel, R S appears and fills in as the purple RS matrix, with its columns taken from the right plane's final arrows. Both final grids are held side by side. Then a muted outline of the right grid and its arrows slides over the left plane. e1 points to the diagonal in one and straight up in the other, and the two grids clearly do not match. The outline slides back and fades. A ≠ sign appears between SR and RS in the panel.
key_points: Shearing first leaves e1 alone and tilts e2. Rotating afterwards carries both on
Reading off the final arrows gives RS
Laid on top of each other, the two final grids disagree: e1 lands in different places
SR ≠ RS: the same two motions in a different order give a different map
elements: grid_SR: left plane in the rotate-then-shear position, with e1 and e2
grid_RS: right plane in the shear-then-rotate position, with e1 and e2
e1: green arrows in both planes
e2: red arrows in both planes
SR: teal matrix in the panel
RS: purple matrix in the panel, with ≠ between SR and RS
scenes.ends_with: Two planes side by side: on the left the rotate-then-shear grid, on the right the shear-then-rotate grid, each with its green e1 and red e2. The panel shows the teal SR ≠ the purple RS.

scenes.title: Usually different, sometimes equal
scenes.purpose: AB ≠ BA in general, but not always. Two rotations give the same result in either order, so whether the order matters depends on the motions.
scenes.shows: Both planes smoothly undo their motions back to the identity at the same time. In the panel, SR ≠ RS moves to the top and becomes smaller. On the left, the plane rotates by a quarter turn, pauses, then rotates by an eighth of a turn. On the right, it rotates by an eighth of a turn, pauses, then rotates by a quarter turn. These play one after the other, never at the same time. Both final grids are held side by side, and they look the same. A muted outline of the right grid slides onto the left plane and lines up exactly with it, arrow for arrow. It slides back and fades. Under SR ≠ RS, the panel now shows the two rotation products in both orders, joined by an = sign. The final frame holds both comparisons in the panel: unequal for the shear and rotation, equal for the two rotations.
key_points: Two rotations done in either order land the grid in the same place
So some pairs of matrices do commute
Non-commutativity means 'not in general', not 'never'
elements: grid_left: left plane after the quarter turn and then the eighth turn
grid_right: right plane after the eighth turn and then the quarter turn
e1: green arrows in both planes
e2: red arrows in both planes
comparison: SR ≠ RS above, and the two rotation products with = below, in the panel
scenes.ends_with: Two planes rotated by the same total angle, matching exactly, each with green e1 and red e2. The panel shows SR ≠ RS above and the equality of the two rotation products below. Hold still.

teaching_plan.learning_goal: The student can explain why the product BA is the matrix of doing A first and then B. They can work out BA without a formula by tracking where e1 and e2 land: the columns of A get carried along by B. They can say why AB and BA usually differ, using the rotation and shear as the example: doing two motions in a different order moves the grid somewhere different.
prerequisites: A linear map of R^2 is fully determined by where it sends e1 and e2
The columns of a matrix are the images of e1 and e2 (column 1 = A e1, column 2 = A e2)
How to compute a matrix–vector product A v and read it as moving the vector v
Seeing a 2×2 matrix as a motion of the whole grid (grid lines stay straight, parallel and evenly spaced, and the origin stays fixed)
Recognising R = [[0,-1],[1,0]] as a 90° counterclockwise rotation and S = [[1,1],[0,1]] as a horizontal shear
teaching_plan.key_insight: Doing one motion after another is a single motion, so it has one matrix. To find that matrix, you only need to watch where e1 and e2 finally land. That is why column i of BA is B applied to column i of A, and why the order matters.
misconceptions: Reading BA left to right as 'first B, then A' instead of 'first A, then B' (it acts on v from the right, like B(A v))
Thinking matrix multiplication is entry by entry ([[a,b],[c,d]]·[[e,f],[g,h]] = [[ae,bf],[cg,dh]])
Assuming order doesn't matter because ordinary number multiplication is commutative (expecting SR = RS)
Believing that composing two maps needs a new computation for every point, instead of just following e1 and e2 (forgetting that the composite is still linear)
Mixing up the column rule: thinking column i of BA is A times column i of B
Overcorrecting to 'AB is never equal to BA', when it only fails in general and some pairs, like two rotations, do commute
teaching_plan.concrete_example: The 90° rotation R and the horizontal shear S act on the grid of the plane, with e1 drawn in one colour and e2 in another. Rotate first and then shear: e1 goes to (0,1) and then to (1,1), and e2 goes to (-1,0), where the shear leaves it alone. Reading off the final arrows gives SR = [[1,-1],[1,0]]. In the reverse order, shear first and then rotate: e1 stays at (1,0) and is rotated to (0,1), while e2 is sheared to (1,1) and rotated to (-1,1). That gives RS = [[0,-1],[1,1]]. Put side by side, the two final grids are visibly different, and e1 ends up at (1,1) in one and (0,1) in the other.

arc.step: Doing R and then S is a motion of the plane you can watch from start to finish, and the end result still looks like a linear map: straight, parallel, evenly spaced grid lines and a fixed origin.
arc.why_now: This rests only on the prerequisite picture of a matrix as a grid motion. It raises the question the rest of the film answers: if the end result is one linear map, what is its matrix?
arc.visual_idea: The grid with coloured e1 and e2 rotates 90° (R), pauses, then shears (S). Then the animation replays as one smooth motion from the original grid straight to the final grid, with a ghost of the original left behind. A caption asks: 'Is this one linear map? Which matrix?'

arc.step: Because the composite is linear, its matrix comes from tracking only e1 and e2 through both motions. That gives SR = [[1,-1],[1,0]].
arc.why_now: It reuses the earlier lesson that columns are the images of e1 and e2, now applied to a two-stage motion. The answer is found by watching before any product formula appears.
arc.visual_idea: Leave just the two basis arrows. e1 swings to (0,1) under R, then slides to (1,1) under S, and its trail is kept. e2 swings to (-1,0) under R, then stays put under S because it lies on the x-axis, and that pause is highlighted. The two final arrows drop into a matrix bracket as its columns: [[1,-1],[1,0]].

arc.step: The product of two matrices is defined to be the matrix of this composite: (BA)v = B(Av) for every v. The single matrix SR does in one step what R and then S do in two.
arc.why_now: Only now, after the composite matrix has been seen and read off, does it get a name and a definition. Name things after they have been seen.
arc.visual_idea: A sample vector v (say (2,1)) takes two routes on a split screen. The top route applies R, then S, as two hops. The bottom route applies the single matrix SR in one hop. Both land on the same point. The equation (SR)v = S(Rv) is written underneath, with arrows linking each side to its route.

arc.step: Column rule: column i of BA is B applied to column i of A. Column i of A is where A sent e_i, and B just carries it further.
arc.why_now: Step 2 already did this, so the rule is a summary of what was watched, not a new trick. Stating it now blocks entrywise multiplication and the A-times-columns-of-B mix-up before any computing.
arc.visual_idea: R and S are written side by side, and R's first column (0,1) is highlighted in e1's colour. It lifts out, passes through S like a machine, and comes out as (1,1), which slots into column 1 of SR. The same happens for column 2: (-1,0) becomes (-1,0). Briefly, a wrong entrywise 'product' of R and S flashes up, and its grid is drawn: it doesn't match the composite motion we watched, so it gets crossed out.

arc.step: Order convention: in BA, the matrix next to the vector acts first. So BA means first A, then B, read right to left.
arc.why_now: The student has now written SR for 'rotate, then shear'. The mismatch with left-to-right reading is clear and needs fixing before the order is reversed.
arc.visual_idea: The expression S R v, with v on the right. An arrow sweeps right to left: v is first grabbed by R (the grid rotates in a small inset), then by S (the inset grid shears). A left-to-right reading 'S first' is played in a faded side panel and leads to a different picture, a teaser for the next step.

arc.step: Reversing the order gives a different motion and a different matrix: RS = [[0,-1],[1,1]], which is not SR. Order matters.
arc.why_now: This is the key insight in its sharpest form. All the tools are ready (tracking e1 and e2, the column rule, the right-to-left order), so the student can predict the result and then see it confirmed.
arc.visual_idea: Split screen, both starting from the same grid. Left: rotate, then shear. Right: shear, then rotate. The two play at the same time. On the right, e1 is untouched by the shear and then rotates to (0,1), while e2 is sheared to (1,1) and then rotates to (-1,1). The two final grids sit next to each other, then one is laid over the other: e1 points to (1,1) in one and (0,1) in the other, so they clearly don't match. The matrices SR and RS appear under each panel.

arc.step: AB ≠ BA in general, but not always. Some pairs of motions, like two rotations, give the same result in either order. Non-commutativity is a fact about motions, not a rule that products are never equal.
arc.why_now: This consolidates the insight by marking its limits, and it stops the 'never equal' overcorrection. It also links to the exercise of computing RS and SR and checking that they differ.
arc.visual_idea: A quick second split screen: rotate 90° then 45°, versus rotate 45° then 90°. Both grids end in the same place and overlap exactly. Then a short everyday contrast: a book is rotated then flipped, versus flipped then rotated, and ends up in different poses. Final frame: the shear-and-rotation panels (different) next to the two-rotations panels (same), labelled 'usually different, sometimes equal'.

context.source_title: Linear Algebra, Lecture 3: Linear maps, matrices and determinants
context.topic_summary: Multiplying matrices means doing one linear map after another. BA means 'first A, then B', and each column of BA is B applied to the matching column of A. Because order matters for motions, AB ≠ BA in general.
